Image Segmentation

1. Explanation:

Image segmentation means splitting an image into several "chunks" or regions so each chunk contains pixels that are similar. Often, each region will correspond to part of an object or an entire object (like a car, tree, or person) in a scene.

2. Analogy:

Imagine a coloring book: before coloring, someone has already drawn the outlines for each object (sky, trees, animals). Segmentation is like drawing those outlines.

3. Diagram Description:

Show a photo of a street scene. Next to it, show the same image with colored overlays for different regions (blue for sky, gray for road, red for buildings).

4. Key Points:

•  Segmentation breaks down images into meaningful sections using information like

color, brightness, texture, or pixel location.

• It's used to find boundaries and objects so we can analyze them better.

Segmentation—First Step in Image Analysis

Segmentation is typically the first step when a computer needs to understand an image. It takes raw pixels and starts turning them into "objects," which can then be described, analyzed, or classified.

Think of looking at a LEGO pile: before you can build, you sort the pieces by type

(color/shape). Segmentation is that sorting.

Image of a pile of multicolored LEGOs labeled "pixels," then sorted piles labeled "objects."

4. Algorithm Types:

• Thresholding: Separate using pixel values.
•  Edge-based: Find borders where pixel values change sharply.

•  Region-based: Group pixels that have similar values and are near each other.

•  Can be automatic (unsupervised) or manual (supervised).

Color-Based Segmentation—Three Categories

1. Explanation:

Instead of just using brightness, you can use color to decide how to group pixels. There are three main ways to do this (exact categories may depend on the class, but frequently include):

•  Color thresholding (selecting a range of colors),

•  Clustering in color space (grouping similar colors together),

•  Region growing (picking a color seed and expanding to similar neighbors).

2. Analogy:

Like sorting M&Ms into bowls by their color.

3. Diagram Description:

Picture of multicolored candies, then the candies sorted into separate bowls.

Semantic Segmentation (Meaningful Regions)

With semantic segmentation, every pixel in the image gets a label indicating which type of object it belongs to (car, road, sky, etc).

It's like a map where every region is labeled: "Here be a forest. Here be a river."

Show an image and then the same image where colors/labels overlay every region (blue for sky, green for grass, etc).
Segmentation Methods

1. Explanation:

Different algorithms exist for splitting up images:

•  Active contours (Snakes, Scissors, Level Sets):

Flexible lines that move to find object edges (think of tracing around an object).

•   Split and merge methods (Watershed, clustering, graph-based):

Start with big regions and split/merge them based on similarity.

• Thresholding:

Choose cutoffs in brightness/color to separate regions.

•  K-means/Mean shift:

Group pixels into clusters (like sorting marbles by color).

•  Graph cuts/Normalized cuts:

Treat an image as a graph, cut "weak" connections to separate parts.

2. Comparative Example:

•  Thresholding is simple but only works well if object and background are clearly

different.

•  Active contours can find complex shapes, good for objects with irregular outlines.

3. Diagram Description:

Draw a flowchart with each method as a block, small sketch next to each showing result.

Segmentation by Thresholding—Otsu's Method

Thresholding splits an image by separating bright from dark regions. Otsu's method automatically picks the best spot by making the pixels within each group as similar as possible.

2. Analogy:

It's like dividing a mixed class into two groups so that each group is as similar as possible

(e.g., by height).
A graph (histogram) of pixel values—then draw a vertical line at the "threshold" splitting the two tallest peaks.

4. Step-by-Step:

•  Compute the histogram of grayscale image.

• For every possible threshold, calculate the "spread" (variance) within each group.

•  The "Otsu" threshold will be where these variances are minimized (groups are most

"tight").

Thresholding with Otsu's Method

1. Explanation:

When you look at a grayscale image, you can draw a histogram to see how many pixels have each possible brightness (gray value). Otsu's method chooses a threshold where this histogram can be "split" into two clear groups (for example: dark background, bright foreground).

2. Analogy:

Imagine a mountain range. You want to draw a fence at the lowest point between two peaks to split the land into two valleys—the goal is that each side is as "uniform" as possible (all pixels on the left look similar, all pixels on the right too).

3. Diagram Description:

Show the histogram of gray values, with a line at the selected threshold (fence in the valley).

Show parts of the image before and after thresholding.

4. Step-by-step:

1. Draw histogram from image.

2.  Try every possible threshold (test every "fence").

3. For each, calculate how spread out (different) the pixels are on each side.

4.  Pick the threshold that gives the lowest spread (most similar within each group).

Binary Segmentation – Foreground vs. Background

Binary segmentation is the ultimate simplification: every pixel is either foreground (object
of interest) or background (everything else) . Usually, this means the result is just black and white.

2. Analogy:

Think of a silhouette: you either see the person or you see the empty space around them, nothing in between.

3. Diagram Description:

Picture of an object, then next to it, the same picture in just two colors (object in white, background in black).

Binary Thresholding – Object Detection

1. Explanation:

Once you have a binary image (just black & white), you can easily find where objects are— this makes them stand out and lets you count or measure them.

Like shining a flashlight through a stencil: only the "object" (hole in the stencil) shows up on the wall.

Show the original image and a binary version with separate blobs for objects.

Binary Image Analysis

In binary image analysis, you use simple images (only 0s and 1s, or black and white) to figure out things like:

•  Where the objects are

•  How many objects there are

•  How big each object is, etc.

It's like counting cookies on a tray after separating them by using a cutter—the tray is empty space, the cookies are what remain.
•  Show an image of cookies on a white tray (objects on a plain background).

•  Show binary code underneath (e.g. 0s for background, 1s for cookies).

Global threshold selection – Threshold too low

Simple Explanation:

A "global" threshold means the same cutoff value is applied everywhere in the image. If it's too low, everything brighter than that value is chosen. This may miss dim parts of the object, or select background noise.

Analogy:

Like setting a metal detector's sensitivity so low you only find very big metal pieces, missing coins and nails.

Image/Diagram:

•  Two black-and-white (binary) images: "Medium threshold" finds more, "High

threshold" finds only the brightest part, missing the rest.

Manual Thresholding

Manually adjusting the threshold value to get the best separation between object and background by visual inspection.

Like turning a dimmer switch until a room looks bright "enough" according to your eyes.

Show before/after binary masks as you adjust the slider.

Local Thresholding

Instead of a single threshold for the whole image, break the image into small areas

("windows") and calculate a separate threshold for each one. This handles changes in lighting or contrast across the image.

Imagine different streetlights along a road: Each section can adjust brightness based on its spot's needs.
Image/Diagram:

Show a thermal image where a red rectangle marks a window. The right shows the result after local (windowed) thresholding—object stands out better.

Steps:

1.  Slide a window over the image.

2. Compute the best threshold in that window (e.g., using Otsu's method).

3. Apply to pixels inside that window.

Local Thresholding Using Edge Information

Simple Explanation:

1.  First, find all the edges in the image (using an "edge detector").

2. Calculate the gray level average along those edges inside a window.

3. Use that as the threshold for just that window.

Analogy:

Like drawing lines around countries on a map, then measuring average altitude for each country to decide flood levels locally.

•   Left: Black image with white edges (Canny detector).

• Arrow points to a window; thresholded result on the right, object stands out sharply.

1. Detect edges.

2. Compute average pixel value along edges (in a window).

3. Use as local threshold for that window.

Edge Image and Local Thresholding

Shows how the edge image guides the determination of the local threshold, only considering a specific window region for thresholding.
Image/Diagram:

•  Edge image.

•  Selected window.

•   Binarized result for just that window.

Object Detection in Video Sequences

Simple Explanation:

Detect moving objects by seeing what's changed between frames:

1. Take a current video frame.

2. Subtract a time-averaged "background" frame.

3. Take the absolute difference ("difference image").

4. Use thresholding (often Otsu) to find where changes are big enough to indicate an

object.

Analogy:

Like spotting a new car parked on a street by comparing today and yesterday's street photos.

•   Left: A video frame.

• Right: Thresholded difference image (white where there's change—e.g., a person

moving).

Steps:

1. Compute (current frame – background).

2. Calculate the absolute value.

3. Threshold the result (Otsu or chosen value).

4. Highlight changed areas.
Segmentation by Clustering (K-means and color clustering)

Simple Explanation:

Instead of just using pixel brightness, look at several features (like color). Pixels with similar features are grouped ("clustered") together.

K-means Clustering Algorithm (Parametric clustering)

Step-by-Step:

1.  Pick the number of clusters, K (often based on how many main regions you expect).

2. Randomly pick K pixels to start as "cluster centers."

3. For every pixel, assign it to the nearest cluster center (using distance in

color/feature space).

4. Calculate the new mean (average) feature values for each cluster to update the

K-means Clustering Algorithm (parametric clustering)

Explanation:

K-means is a method to group pixels by their features (e.g., color or intensity). This way, similar parts of the image are segmented together.

1. Pick K (number of clusters): Decide how many different regions you want in the

image.

2.  Initialize Centers: Randomly choose K pixels as starting cluster "centers."

3. Assign Pixels: Each pixel is assigned to the nearest center (in

color/intensity/feature space).

4. Update Centers: For each cluster, calculate the average of assigned pixels'

features—this becomes the new center.

5. Repeat: Assign and update until assignments stop changing (converge).

Analogy:

Imagine organizing children into three teams for a game. You start by picking three (K) leaders, group everyone by which leader they're closest to, count and re-calculate the average positions, move the leaders, and repeat until no one wants to move teams.

Diagram :
•  Scatter plots of points:

•  Show initial random cluster centers (dots in three colors).

•  Show circles (points) assigned to nearest center, with dotted lines separating

clusters.

•  Show "arrows" as cluster centers move to new averages.

•   Final plot: clusters are neatly separated by straight lines.

K-means Clustering Using Color

Explanation:

Here, the feature used for clustering is color (e.g., RGB values). The algorithm groups pixels based on their color similarity.

Real-World Example:

Like sorting a bowl of Skittles by their color, regardless of their position in the bowl.

Diagram :

•  Show an original image (e.g., two parrots).

• Next to it: a "clustered" version where each main color region is solid (background is

grouped, and each parrot's colors are distinct).

Active Contours (Snakes, Intelligent Scissors, Level Sets)

Active contours are curves (or lines) that evolve to "hug" object boundaries in an image.

They start near the target object and move automatically to tightly fit its shape, influenced by edge strength in the image.

Varieties:

• Snakes: Curves (splines) that slither toward strong edges.

•   Intelligent Scissors: User draws rough outline, algorithm tweaks the curve to stick

to nearby edges.

•  Level Sets: More mathematical, evolve a shape to match object boundaries (can

handle splitting or merging objects).
How it Works:

1. Place an initial curve close to the object.

2.  In each iteration, the curve is adjusted inward/outward to stick to strong image

edges (where brightness or color changes a lot).

3. Stops when curve fits the boundary well.

Analogy:

Like a rubber band placed loosely around a stone. As you let go of the band, it tightens and wraps snugly around the stone's edge.

Diagram:

•  Show an image (person or animal) with an initial "loose" curve.

•  Show the same curve after several steps, "pulling in" and matching the true

boundary.

Image Description :

• One example: Curve around an object (e.g., around a squirrel or a person's head).

•  Shows markers/normals indicating the direction the curve is moving each step.

•   Final result: curve matches object's outline perfectly.

Final Example: Segmentation Result

Explanation:

All the described methods (thresholding, clustering, contour finding) aim to produce a result where objects are clearly separated from the background.

•  Original image next to segmented image (in false colors or binary), e.g.,

Autumn leaves on pavement: left — natural photo, right — leaves are bright yellow, background is dark blue.

Real-World Value:

Easy to measure, count, classify or further analyze individual objects (e.g., for quality inspection, biology, driverless cars, etc.).
Split and Merge Methods — Principles

Key Concepts

•  Region-based methods: Segment images by grouping similar pixels into regions.

•  Recursive splitting: Keep dividing (splitting) the image into smaller regions until

each one is uniform by some criteria (like color or texture).

•  Hierarchical merging: Start with many small regions or single pixels and merge

them if they are similar enough.

•  Combined splitting-and-merging: Algorithms often do both—split until

homogeneous, then merge adjacent similar regions.

1. Simple Explanation

•  Imagine an image as a big cake—you can cut it into slices (splitting), or if you have

tiny cake pieces, you can put similar ones together (merging) to form slices.

2. Real-world Analogy

•   Sorting a box of colored buttons:

Splitting: Keep dividing the pile in half by color.

Merging: Start with every button in its own pile, and group those of the same color together.

3. Diagram Idea

•  Draw a big square (original image), split into four squares, and repeat until each

region is one color (splitting).

•  Draw lots of dots grouped into clusters and those clusters merged into larger blobs

(merging).

4. Step-by-step

• Splitting:

1. Check if region is uniform.

2. If not, divide it into subregions.

3. Repeat for each subregion.

• Merging:

1.  Start with pixels or tiny regions.
2. Merge adjacent regions if similar.

3. Repeat until no more merges possible.

5. Types/Categories — Example

•  Watershed, Region splitting (divisive), Merging (agglomerative), Graph-based

(Normalized Cuts/Graph Cuts).

Agglomerative Clustering — Dendrogram and Distance Measures

Key Concepts

• Agglomerative clustering: Merge each data point (pixel or small region) step by

step into larger clusters based on similarity.

•  Dendrogram: A tree diagram showing how clusters merge at each step.

•  Distance Measures: Used to decide which clusters to merge.

1. Simple Explanation

•  Imagine each friend at a party stands alone. The two most similar people start

talking and form a pair, and others join groups step by step—this forms a merging tree.

2. Real-world Analogy

• Making teams in a game, where kids closest in age join together, then teams close in

size merge, shown in a family tree.

3. Diagram Idea

•  Show a dendrogram, where branches merge together stepwise (as in figure), and a

scatter plot with blue and red clusters, arrows showing d_min (closest two) and d_max (furthest two).

4. Step-by-step

•  Calculate distances between every pair of clusters.

•  Merge the pair with the smallest distance.

•  Update the distances (how close are the new clusters?).

•  Repeat until only one cluster or desired number remains.
Normalized Cuts (Graph-based Segmentation)

Key Concepts

•  Graphs: Pixels as nodes, edges weighted by similarity.

•  Normalized Cuts: Splitting the graph so connections inside groups are strong,

between groups are weak.

1. Simple Explanation

•  Think of people as dots connected by lines that are thick if they're friends. Cut the

weakest links to separate the "friend groups."

2. Analogy

• Dividing a classroom into groups for a project by breaking the weakest friendships

(least connection), ensuring that each group is as cohesive as possible.

3. Diagram Idea

•  Draw two clusters of nodes (circles) connected by strong lines inside, weak lines

between, and then a dashed cut splitting the two.

4. Step-by-step

•  Calculate similarities between each pixel and its neighbors.

•  Make a graph connecting similar pixels.

•  Find the cut that, normalized for group size, best separates strong groupings by

cutting weakest links.

5. Types/Comparisons

•  Works well to avoid tiny, unbalanced regions.

•   Differs from standard "minimum cut" methods by normalizing the cut value.

Graph Cuts (Energy Minimization for Segmentation)

•  Graph cut segmentation: Partition pixels into two sets by minimizing an "energy"

function.
•  Energy-based methods: Combine pixel values and region statistics.

•  Binary segmentation: Divides image into foreground and background.

1. Simple Explanation

• Imagine coloring an image with two colors, where you want similar areas to be same

color, and the "cost" of different neighbors is high.

2. Analogy

• Cutting a string of beads into two strings such that beads of similar color are stuck

together, and the cut is made where bead colors change the most.

3. Diagram Idea

•   Picture an image as a network, cut through low-weighted connections, separating

clusters.

4. Step-by-step

1.  Build a graph from the image.

2. Assign "source" (e.g., foreground) and "sink" (background).

3. Assign edge weights based on similarity and likelihood of pixel belonging to

foreground/background.

4. Find the minimum cut that separates source and sink with lowest energy.

Morphological Operations — Erosion and Dilation

Key Concepts

•  Erosion: Shrinks objects by removing edge pixels.

•   Dilation: Expands objects by adding pixels along their edges.

•  Structuring Element: A template shape used to probe the image.

•   Erosion: Like sand wearing down a rock, shrinking shapes.

•   Dilation: Like blowing up a balloon, expanding shapes.
•   Erosion: Trimming the edges of a bush.

•   Dilation: Spraying paint around a stencil to grow the area.

3. Diagram Idea

•  Show a blob, then a smaller version for erosion, and a larger for dilation with

structuring elements sketched.

4. Erosion Steps

1. For each pixel, overlay the structuring element.

2. If the shape fits entirely inside the object, keep the pixel; otherwise, remove it.

5. Dilation Steps

2. If any part overlaps with the object, add pixels around the edge.

Morphological Operations — Opening and Closing

Key Concepts

•  Opening: Erosion followed by dilation. Removes small spots/noise.

• Closing: Dilation followed by erosion. Fills in small holes/gaps.

1. Simple Explanation

•  Opening: Smooths shapes and gets rid of tiny outgrowths.

• Closing: Fills small holes and connects breaks.

2. Analogy

• Opening: Using a comb to remove small tangles from hair.

• Closing: Using putty to fill cracks in a wall.

•  Show a shape with bumps, after opening the bumps disappear. Show a shape with

holes, after closing the holes are filled.

4. Step-by-step

•  Opening:
1. Erode the image (remove small objects).

2.  Dilate the result (restore size).

• Closing:

1.  Dilate the image (fill gaps).

2. Erode the result (restore size).

Examples (Visual Comparison)

•  Original Image: Leaves on a road.

•  Segmented Image: Leaves highlighted in yellow on blue background.

•  After Opening: Small noise removed, sharper leaf shapes.

•  After Closing: Gaps inside leaves filled.

Diagram/Description:

Show a set of images:

1.  Original

2. Segmented

3. After opening

4. After closing

Helps see how segmentation improves and is cleaned by morphological operations.

Summary

Key Takeaways

•  Image Segmentation divides an image into parts/regions.

•  Main techniques:

• Thresholding: Select by pixel values.

• Clustering (Split & Merge, Agglomerative): Group by similarity.

•  Graph-based (Normalized Cuts, Graph Cuts): Complex relationships.
•  Morphological operations: Clean up and adjust segmentation.

It takes raw pixels and starts turning them into "objects," which can then be described, analyzed, or classified. Morphological Operations - Erosion and Dilation Key Concepts • Erosion: Shrinks objects by removing edge pixels. • Dilation: Expands objects by adding pixels along their edges. • • • • Structuring Element: A template shape used to probe the image. • Erosion: Like sand wearing down a rock, shrinking shapes. • Dilation: Like blowing up a balloon, expanding shapes.
